title.narrative: GCAMF Refugees Financial Inclusion Guarantee Program 2019-2022
GCAMF Refugees Financial Inclusion Guarantee Program 2019-2022

description.narrative:
Grameen Crédit Agricole Microfinance Foundation (GCAMF) har tillsammans med UNHCR ansökt om finansiering från Sida om 30 816 003 SEK, budget för teknisk assistans (TA) samt subventionsgaranti både för administration och förväntad förlust, för att genomföra "Programmet för finansiellt inkluderande av flyktingar och värdsamhällen i Uganda" under perioden 2019-2024. Insatsen, som har initierats gemensamt av UNHCR och Sida, syftar till att förbättra försörjningen och motståndskraften för flyktingar och värdsamhällen genom ekonomisk inkludering och ökade försörjningsmöjligheter för flyktingar och värdsamhällen. Detta ska uppnås genom att: 1) främja egenföretagande och inkomstgenererande aktiviteter genom stöd till nystartade företag och utvidgning av befintlig affärsverksamhet genom mikrokreditlån; 2) förbättra flyktingars affärsförmåga och finansiella kunskaper genom tillhandahållande av icke-finansiella tjänster; 3) underlätta flyktingars sysselsättning genom att stödja småföretagens utlåning bland värdbefolkningen i de sektorer där flyktingar, i enlighet med landets lagar, kan anställas.
Programmet har i allmänhet en marknadsbaserad ansats som involverar partnerskap med en specialiserad mikrofinansieringsfond, stiftelsen GCAMF, som kommer att tillhandahålla skuldfinansiering till ett antal leverantörer av finansiella tjänster (Financial Service Providers- FSPer) som är villiga att låna ut till flyktingar. Stiftelsen kommer att tillförsäkras en partiell kreditgaranti från Sida som kommer att tillämpas om FSPerna inte kan fullgöra sina åtaganden som följd av att låntagare inte kunnat återbetala sina lån. Programmet har också en mekanism för teknisk assistans (TA).
Även om interventionen är ett gemensamt initiativ från UNHCR och Sida, är UNHCR inte den huvudsakliga samarbetspartnern för Sida - UNHCR har dock varit, och kommer att vara, en viktig partner i utformningen, planeringen och genomförandet av projektet. Den formella samarbetspartnern är GCAMF, en stiftelse registrerad i Luxemburg i september 2008, vars uppgift är att bidra till kampen mot fattigdom. GCAMF valdes ut genom ett öppet ansökningsförfarande för mikrofinansieringsfonder som genomfördes av UNHCR redan 2017. Därefter beställde Sida en översyn av GCAMFs interna styrnings- och kontrollsystem. Granskningen genomfördes av KPMG 2017 vars övergripande bedömning var att organisationen har den nödvändiga kapaciteten, kompetensen och systemen för genomförandet av insatsen. I samråd med UNHCR och Sida har GCAMF även identifierat tre finansiella tjänsteleverantörer (FSPer) som de viktigaste genomförande partnerna för projektet i Uganda: BRAC Uganda, VisionFund Uganda och Ugafode. Utbildningar i finansiell kompetens och affärsutveckling kommer också att tillhandahållas av icke-statliga organisationer (NGOer) som har den kompetens och erfarenhet som uppgiften kräver. VisionFund Uganda och BRAC Uganda har NGO-grenar som har erfarenhet av att tillhandahålla sådan utbildning och kapacitetsuppbyggnad. Ugafode FSP kommer att samarbeta med Jesuit Refugee Service (JSR) för att tillhandahålla dessa tjänster. Urvalet av NGOer gjordes av GCAMF och FSPerna i samråd med UNHCR och Sida.
Den totala budgeten för insatsens TA-mekanism är 61 101 746 kr, varav Sida bidrar med 27 094 351 kr (exkl. subventionsbeloppet för förväntad förlust på 2 290 122 kr) och de återstående 34 007 395 kr täcks av FSPerna. Cirka 22 924 229 kr av insatsbudgeten kommer att kanaliseras av GCAMF till FSPerna och 4 170 122 kr kommer att gå till GCAMF direkt.

Grameen Crédit Agricole Microfinance Foundation (GCAMF), in coordination with UNHCR, has applied to Sida for funding of 30,816,003 SEK, TA budget and subsidy for the guarantee, to carry out the financial inclusion program for refugees and host communities in Uganda during the period 2019-2024. The intervention, which has been initiated jointly by Sida and UNHCR, aims at improving livelihoods and resilience of refugees and host communities through financial inclusion and increased livelihood options for refugees and host communities, by: 1) fostering self-employment and income generating activities by supporting start-ups and expansion of existing business activities through micro-credit loans; 2) enhancing refugees' business skills and financial literacy through the provision of non-financial services; 3) facilitating refugees’ employment by supporting small businesses lending among the host population in those sectors where refugees, in accordance with the country´s laws, can be employed.
The program generally follows a market-based approach which involves partnering with a specialized micro-finance foundation, the GCAMF, which will provide debt funding to a number of financial service providers (FSPs) willing to lend to refugees. The Foundation will be recipient of a partial credit guarantee from Sida which will be used in case the FSPs default due to borrowers not being able of repaying back their loan. The program also has a Technical Assistance (TA) facility.
While the intervention is a joint initiative of Sida and UNHCR, UNHCR is not the main cooperation partner though it has been and remains to be an essential partner in the design, planning as well as implementation of the project. The formal cooperation partner is Grameen Crédit Agricole Microfinance Foundation (GCAMF), a Foundation registered in Luxembourg in September 2008. The mission of the Foundation is to contribute to the fight against poverty. GCAMF was selected through a call for applications for microfinance funds that was conducted by UNHCR back in 2017. Subsequently, Sida commissioned a review of its internal management and control system. The review was conducted by KPMG in 2017 and its overall assessment was that the organization has the necessary capacity, competencies and systems for the implementation of the intervention. In consultation with UNHCR and Sida, GCAMF has also identified three financial service providers (FSPs): BRAC Uganda, VisionFund Uganda, and UGAFODE as main implementing partners of the project in Uganda. Financial literacy and business development trainings will also be provided by NGOs who have the competency and the experience the task demands. VisionFund Uganda and BRAC Uganda have NGO wings that have experience in providing such training and capacity building services. Ugafode FSP will work with the Jesuit Refugee Service (JSR) to provide these services. The selection of the NGOs was done by GCAMF and the FSPs in consultation with UNHCR and Sida.
The intervention’s total budget of the TA facility of the program is 61,101,746 SEK, out of which Sida contributes 27,094,351 SEK (excl. the subsidy amount of 2,290,122 SEK) and the remaining 34,007,395 is contributed by the FSPs. Approximately 4,170,122 SEK of the intervention budget will be kept by GCAMF while approximately 22,924,229 SEK will be forwarded from GCAMF to the FSPs.

The overall objective of the intervention is to contribute to the protection and solutions of UNHCR’s persons of concern and host populations by improving their livelihoods and self-reliance through the facilitation of access to credit for business activities. The main expected short-term outcomes of the intervention are: - increased refugees’ access to financial services. - Improved financial understanding, budget management and business skills. - Increased business activities and turnover. - Increased employment among refugees and host community population. As a long-term outcome, the program expects the target communities to have better ability to cope with risks and reduced vulnerability with an ultimate aim of decreasing poverty levels among the beneficiaries. This is also expected to bring down the level of aid dependency among refugees. The intervention will also help in creating incentives for lending of bank funds in protracted refugee situations, and it is hoped to help in freeing up and allowing more resources including donor funding to be spent on acute refugee needs. In terms of beneficiaries, the program plans to benefit 55 000 refugees and 51 000 host community members in intervention focus areas.

Not unexpectedly the programme suffered the negative effects of the COVID-19 pandemic during the first two years of implementation, which led to slower progress of programme activities than originally planned. While the first year of the programme was heavily affected by the COVID-restrictions imposed in Uganda, the implementation of activities have been sped up considerably as from early 2021.
The results achieved by the three Microfinance Institutions (Financial Service Providers, or FSPs) varies between the FSPs and differ in a number of ways when measuring and assessing the reported achievements to date. Looking at the total number of beneficiaries (95,950) who have accessed financial services through the programme (by April 2023), then the programme is largely on-track to reach the planned number of beneficiaries (106,000). This assessment is further supported by recent data presented at the annual meeting ion 29 November 2023 which indicate that the programme targets had been surpassed by the activity end-date in October 2023. However, this data will need to be confirmed in the next narrative report. What is clear, however, is that the results continue to differ between the FSPs with regards to the number of refugees and host community members reached and the average loan size.
The overall results is largely dependent on the fact that one of the three FSPs, namely Visionfund Uganda (VFU), has been granting loans to a much higher number of refugees and host community members than originally planned. By end of April 2023, VFU had been able to reach more beneficiaries (95,950) than planned (12,500), with women constituting the vast majority of VFU clients (73%). VFU is providing loans through a mixture of so called Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) for refugees and individual loans to host community members, and by actively and consciously pushing to digitalise its operations to help expand its reach, reduce operational costs and to make its financial services more easily accessible. The proportion of refugee borrowers in the VFU portfolio is below the intended target, but this is mitigated by their significant overachievement in terms of the number of refugee borrowers (24,402) against the target (7,500) and by the fact that VFU have been able to lend to a much larger number of host community members (71,548) than originally planned (5,000). Due to VFUs rapid expansion and ability to provide financial services in the refugee hosting areas where they operate, the overall programme appears to be on-track.
This means that the two other FSPs, namely UGAFODE and BRAC Uganda Bank Limited (BRAC), are largely underperforming against their targets. Although the proportion of refugees among borrowers is higher in UGAFODEs portfolio, in line with the programme objectives, their results in terms of absolute number of borrowers (4,986) are well below the planned targets (29,500). This is seemingly explained by UGAFODE focusing on a segment of the target populations, namely individuals with more established businesses. This is exemplifed by UGAFODE having a significantly higher average loan size compared to the average loan size of VFU who are reaching far more refugees and host community members. Of concern, however, is that the reported UGAFODE results might be revised downwards in the upcoming narrative report to Sida, because a segment of this loan portfolio was made possible by a GCAMF loan to UGAFODE which will no longer be guaranteed through the Sida guarantee because the loan terms issued by GCAMF did not align with the end-date of the Sida guarantee.
BRAC is the FSP that has had the highest level of underperformance throughout the programme period. This is partly explained by GCAMF and BRAC by referencing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent lockdowns in Uganda, during which BRAC lost a significant proportion of its nationwide business. As a result, the management of BRAC has been focused on recovering nationwide losses and therefore shown little concrete efforts to achieve results within this programme. BRAC has not requested a loan from GCAMF that is covered by Sidas guarantee, nor have they expanded their financial operations in refugee hosting areas as planned, evidenced by only reaching 5,884 people by October 2022 of whom none were refugees. However, there seems to have been some improvements in outreach and expanding access to financial services to refugees in the final year of the programme, with data presented at the annual meeting in November 2023 indicating that BRAC have provided financial services to 11,413 beneficiaries by the programme end-date in October 2023, of which 2,400 are refugees. These figures will need to be confirmed in the next narrative report to Sida while it is still noted that these achievements are, just like UGAFODE, far below the programme targets. Due to being a more established actor on the financial market in Uganda, BRAC was originally assessed as beomg the best-placed FSP to achieve results at-scale and therefore had an original programme target of 64,000 borrowers, with one half of these being refugees. This assumption has since proved false.
Assessing the quality of the loans issued to refugees, there are indications that the overall loan portfolio quality has improved over the course of the programme and that it is currently largely in line with industry standards. This is measured by GCAMF and the three FSPs by using the Portfolio at Risk at 30 days (PAR30) measurement, with data indicating that the portfolio quality for host community borrowers is slightly better when compared with the refugee borrowers. VFU is reporting a higher number of loans at-risk than UGAFODE or BRAC, meaning that there is a higher proportion of borrowers who are at-risk of being unable to repay their loans. Sida's assessment is that this is likely because VGU are less risk-averse than the other FSPs, evidenced by the much higher number of borrowers accessing financial services from VFU. Furthermore, BRAC and UGAFODE have indicated that the lower number of people accessing their financial services is due to the perceived risks involved in granting loans to people without any collateral and to people who might not have stable sources of income.
In addition to the financial services in the form of lending, the three FSPs have also been given funding to provide refugees and host community members with non-financial services in the form of various financial literacy trainings, including the importance of budgeting and saving, business management, VSLA governance and records-keeping and so on. The purpose of these non-financial services has been to enhance overall financial literacy and understanding among the target population, to help foster improved budget management and business skills, and ultimately to improve their access to financial services by making the beneficiaries better prepared when interacting with FSPs. In addition to the financial literacy aspect, BRAC has also offered awareness-raising sessions and trainings to young mothers and girls between 14-24 years old, sensitising them on various protection-related issues, including gender-based violence (GBV), available case management services, survivor-centred assistance and psychosocial support services. Integrating this in their non-financial services work is aimed at reducing protection risks by enhanced awareness and by supporting them to acquire skills that will help generate incomes.
Sida has previously noted and communicated with GCAMF and the three FSPs that they must improve their analysis and reporting around the added-value of these non-financial services and how they contributing to the overall programme objective of enhancing access to financial services. Although there is a strong correlation between the reported number of training participants and borrowers for both VFU and BRAC, it is not immediately clear whether there are any direct linkages or overlap between those accessing non-financial services and the financial services. Sida has repeatedly requested for GCAMF and the FSPs to better describe the linkages between the two and whether those who receive financial literacy trainings are then able to access loans through any of the FSPs, or vice versa. Especially concerning is that UGAFODE has reported a sigficicant variance between the number of people accessing financial literacy trainings and loans, which Sida noted and raised with GCAMF. This variance is explained by poor records management at UGAFODE and its partners, resulting in double-counting and making it impossible to accurately report the number of unique individuals who have accessed non-financial services.
It is therefore clear to say that the programme appears on-track to reach its objectives in terms of the number of refugees and host community members accessing financial services, although Sida notes the varying degree to which the various partners have contributed to reaching the overall target.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
